title: Bring us back
hook: the next asks for return to the Torah and to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, binah, the first thing the Amidah asks for. Your line was first, understanding. Did you ask one more question before deciding? Today, what understanding leads to. Day five hundred eighty-two.

A phone's map app has one phrase it says more patiently than any person ever could. Rerouting. You missed the exit, you took the wrong lane, you ignored it three times in a row. It never says you idiot. It never says go home. It just quietly works out the way back from exactly where you are. The second request of the Amidah is built on the same idea. Once you understand where you are, the next thing to ask for is the way back.
screen: `REROUTING.` → `NEVER: YOU IDIOT.` → `THE WAY BACK FROM WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: The fifth blessing says: bring us back, our Father, to Your Torah. Draw us near, our King, to Your service. And return us in complete teshuvah before You. Blessed are You, who desires teshuvah. Teshuvah is usually translated repentance, but it shares its verb with turning, returning: the same verb as in the Lamentations verse. It's less about feeling terrible and more about changing direction. The blessing echoes the end of the book of Lamentations. In the old Jewish translation: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned." Notice the grammar. The person praying asks God to do the turning. It admits that coming back is hard to do alone. Notice the two names too. First our Father, then our King. The close relationship comes first, then the formal one. Why does this come right after understanding? The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, points to a verse in Isaiah that runs understanding with their heart, return, and be healed, to explain why return comes right after understanding. You can't turn around until you see where you are. And the blessing's ending is gentle: God desires teshuvah. Wants it. Elsewhere the Talmud, in Pesachim 54a, lists teshuvah among seven things created before the world itself. Before anyone could go wrong, the way back was already built in.
screen: `TESHUVAH: TURNING, RETURNING.` · `TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.` · `FIRST FATHER, THEN KING.` · `UNDERSTAND, THEN RETURN.` · then, large: `BRING US BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn back one step. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you've drifted from who you meant to be. A habit that slipped. A friendship you let go quiet. A promise to yourself you stopped keeping. Don't make a plan for the whole road. Just picture the first step back: one text, one page, one walk, one honest sentence. Notice that you can take it from exactly where you are. If you pray, you can ask for help turning. The bell holds the time.
Bring us back. Hashiveinu. The Amidah's fifth blessing, asking for teshuvah, return, to God, who desires it.
Your line: bring us back. Today, take the one step back you pictured, and keep it small enough that you actually take it. Day five hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Hashiveinu, the request for return, is the fifth blessing of the weekday Amidah; the verse from Lamentations it echoes is also sung as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

trapdoor: what you thought: a request to be sorry for your sins.
what it means: a request for help turning around, from the God who wants you back.
what a scholar hears: Lamentations 5:21; Megillah 17b on Isaiah 6:10 for why return follows understanding; Pesachim 54a lists teshuvah among things created before the world.

notes: Lamentations 5:21 quoted as JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Megillah 17b uses Isaiah 6:10 to explain why the request for return follows understanding; the Gemara considers placing healing right after return and rejects it (forgiveness comes first), so the script no longer claims the verse sets the order of blessings four, five and eight. Confirm.
Pesachim 54a: seven things created before the world, including teshuvah; confirm.
Hashiveinu sung at returning the Torah to the ark (the Lamentations verse); confirm phrasing in howItsDone.
Editor review: the sh-u-v root claim now rests on the quoted Lamentations verse (hashiveinu ... venashuvah); trimmed a stock line.
